subject: os
question: Which semaphore operation decrements the semaphore and may block the caller?
options: signal() / V()
wait() / P()
init()
fork()
explanation: wait() (P) decrements the semaphore and blocks if no units are available; signal() (V) increments it and may wake a waiter.

subject: os
question: What is a critical section?
options: A code segment that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one process at a time
A region of memory reserved for the OS
A part of the kernel that handles errors
The first instruction executed at boot
explanation: A critical section touches shared data, so concurrent execution of it by multiple processes must be prevented.

subject: os
question: What is a race condition?
options: Two processes competing for the highest priority
A situation where the outcome depends on the unpredictable order in which concurrent threads access shared data
A deadlock between two threads
A type of scheduling algorithm
explanation: Race conditions arise when unsynchronized threads interleave operations on shared data, producing timing-dependent results.

subject: os
question: What is a mutex lock primarily used for?
options: Ensuring mutual exclusion so only one thread holds the lock at a time
Counting available disk blocks
Translating virtual addresses
Scheduling I/O requests
explanation: A thread acquires the mutex before entering a critical section and releases it on exit, so only one thread is inside at a time.

subject: os
question: A counting semaphore controls access to a pool of 5 identical printers. What should its initial value be?
explanation: A counting semaphore starts at the number of available instances; each wait() takes one and blocks when the count reaches 0.

subject: os
question: In the semaphore-based bounded-buffer (producer-consumer) solution with n slots, what are the initial values of empty, full and mutex?
options: empty = 0, full = n, mutex = 1
empty = 1, full = 1, mutex = n
empty = n, full = n, mutex = 0
empty = n, full = 0, mutex = 1
explanation: Initially all n slots are empty and none are full, and mutex = 1 allows one process at a time to touch the buffer.

subject: os
question: What happens when signal() is called on a monitor condition variable that has no waiting threads?
options: The signal is saved for the next thread that waits
Nothing; the signal has no effect
An exception is raised
The calling thread blocks
explanation: Unlike a semaphore's signal(), which always increments the count, a condition variable's signal() is lost if nobody is waiting.

subject: os
question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three requirements of a correct critical-section solution?
options: Mutual exclusion
Preemption of the process in the critical section
Progress
Bounded waiting
explanation: A correct solution must provide mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting; preempting the lock holder is not a requirement.

subject: os
question: Peterson's solution to the critical-section problem uses which shared variables?
options: A single semaphore
A boolean flag array and an integer turn
A test_and_set lock
A monitor and a condition variable
explanation: In Peterson's two-process solution, flag[i] signals intent to enter and turn decides who goes first when both want in.

subject: os
question: What property of the test_and_set() hardware instruction makes it usable for building locks?
options: It disables all interrupts permanently
It runs only in user mode
It executes atomically
It is faster than a regular load
explanation: test_and_set reads the old value and sets the word to true as one indivisible step, so only one thread can see false and take the lock.

subject: os
question: What is the key conceptual difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
options: A mutex can count above 1
A binary semaphore can only be used in kernel mode
A mutex has ownership: only the thread that locked it should unlock it
A mutex cannot block threads
explanation: A mutex is owned by the locking thread, while any thread can signal a binary semaphore, which also makes semaphores useful for signaling between threads.

subject: os
question: When is a spinlock most appropriate?
options: On a single-CPU system with long critical sections
When the lock will be held for several seconds
When the waiting thread must sleep
On a multiprocessor when the lock is held only for a very short time
explanation: Spinning avoids the cost of two context switches, which pays off only when the lock holder, running on another CPU, will release it very soon.

subject: os
question: A counting semaphore S is initialized to 10. Then 6 wait (P) and 4 signal (V) operations are performed. What is the final value of S?
explanation: Each P decrements and each V increments, so S = 10 - 6 + 4 = 8 (the value never reaches 0, so nothing blocks).

subject: os
question: What guarantee does a monitor provide?
options: Only one thread can be active inside the monitor at a time
All threads run in parallel inside it
Deadlock can never occur
Condition variables keep a count of signals
explanation: A monitor enforces mutual exclusion on its procedures automatically; condition variables then let threads wait inside it for specific conditions.

subject: os
question: In the first readers-writers solution (readers have priority), what problem can occur?
options: Readers can starve
Two writers can write at the same time
Readers and writers can access the data at the same time
Writers can starve if readers keep arriving
explanation: As long as at least one reader is active, new readers get in right away, so a steady stream of readers can keep a writer waiting forever.

subject: os
question: What is priority inversion?
options: A low-priority process permanently gets a higher priority
The scheduler reverses its priority queue
Two processes swap priorities at each context switch
A high-priority task waits on a lock held by a low-priority task, which is preempted by medium-priority tasks
explanation: The high-priority task is effectively delayed by unrelated medium-priority work, because the low-priority lock holder cannot run.

subject: os
question: What is the standard solution to priority inversion?
options: Priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily inherits the priority of the highest-priority waiter
Aging
Increasing the time quantum
Using spinlocks instead of mutexes
explanation: With inherited priority, medium-priority tasks cannot preempt the lock holder, so it finishes quickly, releases the lock and drops back to its original priority.

subject: os
question: Which real-world incident is the textbook example of priority inversion?
options: The Mars Pathfinder lander's repeated system resets
The Therac-25 accidents
The Y2K bug
The Ariane 5 launch failure
explanation: On Pathfinder, a low-priority task holding a bus mutex blocked a high-priority task, which triggered watchdog resets; enabling priority inheritance in VxWorks fixed it.

subject: os
question: In the naive dining-philosophers solution where each philosopher picks up the left chopstick then the right, what can happen?
options: All philosophers pick up their left chopstick at once and deadlock
Chopsticks are duplicated
Starvation is impossible
Two neighbors eat at the same time
explanation: Each philosopher holds one chopstick and waits for the next one, forming a circular wait; asymmetric pick-up order or allowing at most 4 at the table avoids it.
